payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
Being scanned without consent and being required to produce a record are the same experience from where the person stands. A voluntary record is useful partly because the missing one says nothing, and a duty to produce one turns every blank into an answer.

Two impositions, one shape

A verdict arrives about work you did, produced by a process you never agreed to, and your options are to accept it or argue with a number. Replacing the number with a chain improves the evidence considerably. It does not change who decided that you would be assessed.

Detection is easy to object to because it is so plainly done to people. Since June, anyone can point a free Deezer tool at playlists on twenty streaming services, and nothing in the process involves the artist whose track is being judged. A provenance requirement would be done to people as well, and would be far easier to defend, which makes it the more dangerous of the two rather than the safer. Anything strong enough to settle a dispute is strong enough to be demanded, and the case for demanding it writes itself. The record is cheap, the argument runs, honest contributors have nothing to conceal, so why not require it.

Because of what a requirement does to everyone who does not have one.

A duty makes the blank speak

The IFPI and RIAA labeling scheme announced in July is voluntary by design. The services that would enforce it did not sign the announcement.

Two things are already known about what a missing declaration contains. One is that a blank is consistent with several situations at once and no downstream scrutiny separates them. The other is that the tracks most needing a label will never carry one. Both treat the uselessness of the blank as a finding. It is also a protection, and that part goes unstated.

Under a voluntary scheme, having no record protects the person who simply never engaged with any of this, which is most people. The blank is unreadable, so nothing can be read into it.

A mandate removes that. Once producing a record is a duty, failing to produce one stops being silence and becomes non-compliance, and non-compliance reads as an answer. The several indistinguishable cases collapse into a single interpretation, not because a verifier learned anything, but because a rule was written. The evidence did not improve. The default did.

There is a distinction underneath this that the design depends on. Recording that no identity was present is a fact, and a system should record it plainly, with the same weight it gives to presence. Reading that fact as guilt is an inference, and nothing obliges anyone to make it. A requirement makes it automatically, on everybody, at once.

A voluntary record still has a cost

Voluntary does not mean costless, and pretending otherwise would be the weak version of this argument. A distributor holding two deliveries, one with a chain and one without, will prefer the first. No mandate was needed to produce that outcome, and none would be needed to deepen it. A studio with capture infrastructure will have records. Someone working alone on a laptop will not, until the record accrues with no effort and no expense at the moment of honesty. That is why cheapness carries the whole design.

So the claim is narrower than it first sounds. Some people will be worse off for having no record, and a market will sort them without anyone imposing a thing. That is a real cost and it is still the better trade, because the alternative is a probabilistic accusation that lands on everyone with nothing available to answer it.

What nobody should face is a rule instructing them to produce a record or be treated as though they had failed to. A record is worth something because a person chose to make it. Compel it and you have built another institution while claiming to have removed one.

References

IFPI, RIAA, A2IM, WIN, IMPALA, the Recording Academy, SAG-AFTRA and Human Artistry Campaign. Joint announcement of a unified approach to voluntary generative AI track labeling, July 10, 2026. ifpi.org

Agence France-Presse. "Music industry launches AI-generated content labels." July 10, 2026. jamaicaobserver.com (syndicated)

Music Business Worldwide. "After licensing its AI detection tech to the music industry, Deezer now lets listeners scan their own playlists for AI-generated tracks." June 2026. musicbusinessworldwide.com

DJ Mag. "AI-generated music surpasses 50% of daily uploads on Deezer." July 21, 2026. djmag.com
payload.title: Provenance has to stay refusable
